## Trip Data
The dataset was first inspected to get an overview of the datatypes and find
potential issues. This revealed that several numeric columns were incorrectly stored as strings 
and that the timestamp columns were not yet in datetime format. Both were corrected during preprocessing.
Additionally, the dataset contained no duplicated rows or trip identifiers. Furthermore, several implausible
trips were identified and removed during cleaning. These included trips with zero or negative distance (528447 trips) and trips with a 
duration of less than 60 seconds (381488 trips), as these trips are likely erroneous. Overlapping trips with the same taxi identifier 
were also removed (28320 trips) based on the assumption that these result from recording errors.
Price attributes were also validated by checking for and removing trips with zero or negative fares (1455 trips) and whether there are 
negative tips, tolls or extras (0 trips). 

The dataset was also checked for missing values, revealing that 0.18% of the non-spatial data was missing. Due to the negligible share, these rows were dropped. Because of privacy reasons, the spatial data showed many more missing values with census tract data missing for approximately 55% of trips. In these cases, the less granular community area is recorded instead, meaning spatial information is almost always available at either the census tract or community area level (@fig-trips-by-location-data). 

The numeric columns were checked for outliers using boxplots (@fig-trip-outlier-boxplot) and removed using 
the z-score as a statistical solution. Observations with a z-score exceeding a threshhold of 2 in any numeric 
column were considered outliers and removed. A threshold of 2 was chosen over the more common value of 3 to remove a larger share of extreme values, 
which was deemed acceptable given the large remaining dataset size.
This resulted in 444102 rows, or 7.18%
of the data at that point being removed, leaving the set with roughly 5.7 million rows.

Starting from the outlier-cleaned trip data, spatial fields were finalised through a series of steps. First, trips lacking any spatial information (census tract, community area, coordinates) for either pickup or dropoff location were removed.
Second, trips starting or ending outside of Chicago (@fig-trips-outside-chicago) were dropped using the official community area boundaries as the city outline. 
Third, for all trips with missing community area information, this information was filled using the census tract data, such that the community area is available for all trips and can be used as spatial unit (@fig-community-area-distribution). 
Additionally, H3 hexagons were visualized at multiple levels, 5,6,7 and 8 (@fig-h3-distribution-plots). Resolution 5 was too coarse (only 8 hexagons for Chicago) and resolution 8 implied more spatial precision than the data supports given that coordinates are community area or census tract centroids. Based on that, hexagon IDs at resolution 6 and 7 were assigned to each row with a special approach. Since the trips only carry the single centroid coordinate of their community area, assigning hexagons directly from these coordinates would make all of these trips collapse onto the same point, potentially leaving hexagons with zero trips and a uneven distribution. To avoid this, trips were instead spread out across the whole community area before being assigned to a hexagon, resulting in a smoother, way more realistic distribution across the map (@fig-h3-centroid-vs-area-weighted). Finally, together with the weather dataset, a merged dataset based on the starting hour of the trip was created.

## Supplementary Data
Before the merge, the weather dataset was filtered to the year 2025 to match the trip data, and timestamps were converted from UTC to Chicago local time. A duplicate timestamp and a missing timestamp 
were identified, which can both be attributed to the daylight saving time transition, and were therefore retained as-is. No further cleaning was required. For the POI data, the raw point locations were aggregated into spatial features for 
each community area and H3 hexagon at resolutions 6 and 7. Depending on the category, either a distance or a density feature was computed. For categories where proximity is 
most relevant, the distance to the nearest POI was calculated, while for categories where concentration matters more, the number of POIs per km² within each spatial unit was used  (@fig-poi-features-ca).

## Aggregated Demand Dataset

For predictive modeling, the merged dataset was aggregated into a demand dataset where each row represents one spatio-temporal unit. Trips were grouped by time bucket 
and spatial cell. To ensure complete coverage, zero-demand rows were added for every spatial cell and time bucket 
combination with no recorded trips. Four temporal resolutions (1h, 2h, 6h, 24h) and three spatial resolutions (H3 resolution 6, H3 resolution 7, community area) were 
combined, resulting in 12 datasets. Each row was enriched with temporal features (hour of day, day of week, month, season, public holidays), city-wide weather 
conditions averaged per time bucket, and static POI features describing the character of each spatial cell. Additionally, idle  time was computed as the time between consecutive trips for the same taxi.
Gaps exceeding 4 hours were treated as off-duty periods and excluded. Cyclical temporal features such as hour of day, day of week, and month were encoded 
using sine and cosine transformations to preserve their circular nature.
